newsitem.title: USA: US econ growth seen at 2.1 pct a year - UCLA study.
newsitem.headline: US econ growth seen at 2.1 pct a year - UCLA study.

text.p: The U.S. economy is expected to grow at an annual rate of 2.1 percent until the end of the decade, according to a report published Wednesday by UCLA economists.

Rajeev Dharwan, an economist at the University of California at Los Angeles's forecasting project, said the projection is based on a labor force growing slightly faster, a significant rise in private capital and the conjecture that lower communications costs will provide a modest boost to the pace of technological change.
Between 2000 and 2010, the study predicts U.S. economic growth will accelerate to 2.4 percent annually.
Inflation should remain in check, with the consumer price index expected to increase 2.6 percent annually from 1995 to 2010, Dharwan said.

Dharwan's outlook calls for a balanced budget by 2010, reinforcing the need for a strict monetary policy by the Federal Reserve Bank. The 30-year U.S. Treasury bond should yield about 6.7 percent over the next 15 years, the report added.
Faster technological change should cause higher labor productivity from 1995 to 2010, with non-farm productivity expected to rise 1.5 percent annually.
--business fixed investment will rise as a percentage of gross domestic product from 10.4 percent up to the end of the decade to 13 percent after 2000;
--the growth of private business fixed capital stock should accelerate to 4.5 percent annually over the next 15 years;
--an increase in consumption as a share of real GDP;
--the U.S. will continue importing more than it exports.

The report is based on the "endogenous growth" model, popularized by economist Paul Romer in a 1986 paper. The theory states technological growth comes from within the model, causing "spillovers" and increasing returns across the economy.
The spillovers allow companies to benefit from the technological advances of another company without having to duplicate the orginal effort.
Under the more commonly used economic growth model, as pioneered by Robert Solow in the 1950s, technological growth comes from outside the model.
Because of the spillover effect, the endogenous growth model supports forecasts of higher economic growth than projected by the Solow model.
